newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Asia security talks paper over differences on Burma.
newsitem.headline: Asia security talks paper over differences on Burma.

text.p: Foreign ministers from major Asian and Western nations on Sunday papered over their differences on Burma while "expressing concern" over the political turmoil in Cambodia after a day-long conference on Asian security issues.

The contentious issue of Burma and its admittance on Wednesday to the Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN) was barely mentioned in an 11-page statement issued at the end of the meeting, held at a resort hotel in a water theme park on the outskirts of Kuala Lumpur.

But U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright led a chorus of voices among the 21 foreign ministers at the ASEAN Regional Forum (ARF) -- including Burma's -- who bemoaned the pace of reform in Burma.

"Now that the choice has been made, we must insist that we work together to promote conditions within Burma that will lead towards true democracy and permit its genuine integration into this region," she said, referring to Burma's membership of ASEAN.

Burma was also the only nation in ASEAN "where the government protects and profits from the drug trade....Drug money is laundered with such impunity in Burma that it taints legitimate investment," she added.

Conference chairman, Malaysian Foreign Minister Abdullah Badawi, acknowledged that strong concerns were expressed about Burma's lukewarm reform effort. But he told a news conference at the end of the meeting the ARF endorsed ASEAN's policy of "constructive engagement" with Rangoon.

He acknowledged that Burma's presentation to the group had not gone down very well -- Luxembourg Foreign Minister Jacques Poos, whose country currently holds the European Union presidency, said afterwards he did not think Burmese Foreign Minister Ohn Gyaw's statement "was credible".
Abdullah said Burma "understands very well we have this constructive engagement policy with them".
Southeast Asian diplomats said that Burma, which shares borders with China, India and ASEAN member Thailand, was strategically too important to be isolated.
The conference endorsed ASEAN's efforts to mediate a solution to Cambodia's troubles.
"The ministers expressed concern over the latest developments on the situation in Cambodia," the statement said.
It took note of what it said were assurances by Cambodian Foreign Minister Ung Huot "that Cambodia welcomed ASEAN's role in helping restore political stability in Cambodia."

ASEAN has sought assurances from Cambodian strongman Hun Sen that he is willing to accept ASEAN mediation to help end the political crisis in his country. There was no mention of Hun Sen in Sunday's statement.

Abdullah said no time had been set for the mediation mission, which will be undertaken by three ASEAN foreign ministers. He reiterated that ASEAN was awaiting clarification from Hun Sen that the mediation effort would be truly welcomed.
"There was some confusion," he said referring to conflicting reports from Phnom Penh about ASEAN's role. "It is very difficult to take a decision based on reports which are very conflicting."
Australian Foreign Minister Alexander Downer said a "strong consensus" had emerged in the discussions that ASEAN should take the lead in Cambodian diplomacy.
"What is particularly interesting is the emergence of a consensus which includes in that consensus, countries such as China and the U.S.," Downer said.

Albright in her statement to the group said it was urgent that ASEAN focus on Burma and take other steps to ensure stability in Asia, for "although this region is experiencing an unprecedented period of peace and prosperity, its continued security is not guaranteed".

"A number of territorial and political problems could spark conflict if left unattended. The transnational dangers posed by weapons proliferation, terrorism, narcotics and crime threaten us all," she said.

The ARF statement also called on all states that have not ratified the Chemical Weapons Convention to do so. It welcomed the adoption of the Comprehensive Test Ban Treaty, and supported efforts to get rid of land mines and other unexploded ordnance and rehabilitate the victims.
It welcomed four-party talks between North and South Korea, China and the United States "which could pave the way to a permanent peace on the Peninsula".

The statement said the four-year-old ARF, which includes the nine ASEAN nations, 10 major Asian and Western powers plus observers Cambodia and Papua New Guinea, had "developed into an important forum for multilateral security dialogue and cooperation in the region".
ASEAN comprises Malaysia, Thailand, Singapore, Indonesia, the Philippines, Vietnam, Brunei, Burma and Laos.
The other ARF members are China, the United States, Japan, Russia, the European Union, India, South Korea, Australia, Canada and New Zealand.
